sweep_summary: kota1275 (Kota Bangun Kutai Malay) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Sugiyono 2007 (LOT OS 9 ch.7, open access, already held by the project from the teng1267 check and re-read; copy now at, is a statement-vs-question intonation study whose 14 speakers were all lifelong Tenggarong residents (p.153); it states no word-stress rule and only relays Suryadikara et al. 1979:10 ('no suprasegmental phonemes, although. certain speech sounds are lengthened', p.151). Glottolog's assignment of it to [mqg] is doubtful; it belongs to teng1267 [vkt]. Extra Google Books probing this search of works with stress in the title surfaced Jaludin Chuchu 2003/2005 and a Borneo 2000 BRC paper paraphrasing Collins 1991 on Kota Bangun gemination after a former-schwa penult, plus Collins 1994 JDB 38 ('pemanjangan konsonan dan pemindahan tekanan'); the English 'stress that falls on the penultimate syllable' sentence in those books is credited to Soepomo 1996:11 and concerns Brunei Malay. Best acquisition targets remain Collins 1991 Dewan Bahasa 35, Collins 1993 BRC vol.2 'Kutai Malay: variation and historical change', and Collins 1992 Sari 10 (all print-only; No first-hand Kota Bangun stress statement was read in full

(2) Suryadikara et al. 1979:10 [snippet]: "Fonem suprasegmental ternyata tidak dijumpai dalam BK. new_statements.translation: (2) 'Suprasegmental phonemes turn out not to be found in Kutai (BK). Although there is variation in how words are pronounced, that variation is not phonemic ... e.g. the pronunciation difference between Tenggarong Kutai (BKT) and Kota Bangun Kutai (KKB): KT [manok] [petan] [pisan] vs KKB [mannok] "chicken", [pattan] "dark", [pissan] "banana".' (3) 'For the Kota Bangun dialect in Kutai, Collins (1991) reported that consonant lengthening occurs in the position following Proto-Malayic *ə in disyllabic words ... [the innovations are] shift of stress onto the penultimate syllable, consonant lengthening, and "weighting" of the penultimate vowel (Collins 1994).'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (1) lines 31-34 (p.151, sec. 7.1): 'As regards prosody Suryadikara et al. (1979: 10) mention that there are no supra-segmental phonemes, although there are indications that certain speech sounds are lengthened.' -- verbatim (only the line-break hyphen in 'supra-segmental' differs). Same page lists 'Kutai Tenggarong, Kutai Kotabangun, Kutai Muara Muntai, Kutai Muara Ancalong and Kutai Melak'; p.153 all 14 speakers 'had lived in Tenggarong during their entire life' -> Sugiyono's own data are teng1267, the stress remark is second-hand and about Kutai as a whole. (2) Suryadikara et al. 1979 p.10 snippet: the composite quote is a chain of overlapping Google Books…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive in Kutai Malay (no suprasegmental phonemes, Suryadikara et al. 1979, whose 'BK' explicitly includes the Kota Bangun dialect KKB). For the Kota Bangun variant specifically, Collins (1991, 1994; seen only through Jaludin Chuchu's and Collins's own Malay-language snippets) treats it as a member of the Brunei/East-Borneo Malay group characterised by stress shifted onto the penultimate syllable, with the historically *ə penult triggering gemination of the following consonant ([mannok], [pattan], [pissan]; parrut, tabbəl) — i.e. a stressed, 'weighted' penult. No opened primary source states the placement rule for Kota Bangun in its own words; the modern English primary (Collins 2006, 'Kutai Lakes Malay') apparently does not use the word stress at all.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing found in any opened or snippeted source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as such. Suryadikara et al. 1979 treat KT~KKB differences (gemination) as non-phonemic 'idiolectal variation or local speech melody'; Collins (via Jaludin) restricts gemination to consonants following a PM *ə penult in disyllables, and Collins 2006:42 (snippet) notes that after voiced obstruents the effect can 'reach' the final syllable when it begins with a liquid ([bulət], [bilə]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms/wordlists (Collins's data are elicited wordlists from Kota Bangun, informant Kurdi, since 1987; Borneo 2000 snippet even suggests informants may lengthen only in 'wordlist' style). Sugiyono's own experimental data are sentence intonation from Tenggarong speakers (teng1267), where pitch peaks sit on phrase-final syllables; the Leiden group (van Heuven & van Zanten 2007; Kaufman & Himmelmann 2020/2024 footnotes) tends to file Kutai Malay with the Malay varieties lacking word stress, but that inference rests on the Tenggarong data, not Kota Bangun.
new_statements.identity_note: kota1275 / mqg is the up-river Kutai variety centred on Kota Bangun and the Mahakam lakes (Muara Muntai, Muara Wis, Kenohan, Kembang Janggut..). Collins calls it the 'Kota Bangun variant' (1991-1993) and later 'Kutai Lakes Malay' (2006), contrasting it with (Tenggarong) 'Kutai Malay' = teng1267/vkt, and states the two 'do not appear to be closely related' (Kota Bangun groups with Berau and Brunei Malay through *ə > a and post-schwa gemination). Suryadikara et al. 1979 label it KKB (dialek Kutai Kota Bangun) inside 'bahasa Kutai'. The only on-disk quotable sentence (Sugiyono 2007:151) is itself second-hand and Sugiyono's own speakers are all from Tenggarong (teng1267), so nothing held is a first-hand description of kota1275 prosody. The Leiden 'no word stress' classification of 'Kutai Malay' in handbooks (van Heuven & van Zanten 2007; Kaufman & Himmelmann 2020, 2024) likewise rests on Tenggarong data.
